hints: Removing a leaf is easy. What makes removal hard, and which value could safely take the place of a node that has two children?

Use recursion that returns the new subtree root. Once you find the key: with one or zero children, return the other child; with two, copy in the smallest value of the right subtree (its in-order successor) and delete that value from the right subtree.

1. If the node is null, return null (key absent).
  2. If key is smaller, set left = delete(left, key); if larger, right = delete(right, key).
  3. Found it: if no left child, return right; else if no right child, return left.
  4. Otherwise find the leftmost node of the right subtree, copy its value here.
  5. Set right = delete(right, thatValue) and return the node.

approaches.name: Brute force
approaches.idea: Collect all keys except key and insert them one by one into a fresh tree — the shape will not match the required rule.

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.idea: Search down the path, then fix only the found node using the successor rule; the recursion re-links parents automatically.

explain: In [6,3,9,2,4,null,11] with key 3: 3 < 6, so recurse left and find 3. It has two children, so take the smallest value in its right subtree, which is 4, and copy it into the node. Then delete 4 from that right subtree; 4 is a leaf, so it becomes null. The result is [6,4,9,2,null,null,11]. The successor is larger than everything on the left and smaller than everything else on the right, so the BST order holds. If the key is absent (sample 2, key 7), the recursion hits null and nothing changes.
recognize: Delete from a BST while keeping order → recursive delete with the in-order successor for two-child nodes.
